security_audit.summary: All 94 static findings are false positives caused by Markdown formatting, JavaScript examples, environment configuration, validation messages, and reference links. The skill contains no executable automation, prompt injection, file access, or network behavior. Its JWT example does store reusable refresh tokens in plaintext, creating replay risk after token or database disclosure.

remediation.issue: The JWT example stores reusable refresh bearer tokens in plaintext.
remediation.suggestion: Store only a cryptographic token hash, rotate the refresh token after every use, revoke the previous token, and detect reuse.

semantic_findings.title: Reusable Refresh Tokens Stored in Plaintext
semantic_findings.description: The example stores refresh bearer tokens directly and accepts each token repeatedly until expiry. Token or database disclosure therefore enables session replay.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The code explicitly stores the raw refresh token, checks that same value during refresh, and issues an access token without rotating or invalidating it.

content.user_title: Secure APIs with Practical Design Patterns
content.value_statement: API flaws can expose data, bypass authorization, and disrupt services. This skill provides implementation patterns and review checklists for common API security controls.
actual_capabilities: Explains JWT access tokens, refresh tokens, authentication middleware, and protected routes.
Compares vulnerable SQL construction with parameterized queries and ORM access.
Demonstrates request validation, password hashing, and HTML sanitization.
Shows general, authentication, operation, and user-tier rate limiting patterns.
Provides OWASP-aligned checklists for authorization, data protection, logging, and testing.
limitations: Provides guidance and examples, but does not execute scanners, penetration tests, or dependency audits.
Requires adaptation for the selected framework, identity provider, data model, and deployment environment.
Examples focus mainly on Node.js and Express, with limited GraphQL and WebSocket implementation detail.
Does not replace threat modeling, environment-specific testing, or review by a qualified security professional.

use_cases.title: Design a New API
use_cases.description: Select authentication, authorization, validation, rate limits, and error controls before implementation.

use_cases.title: Review Existing Endpoints
use_cases.description: Compare endpoint behavior against practical controls and the OWASP API Security Top 10.

use_cases.title: Prepare Audit Evidence
use_cases.description: Build a focused checklist for API controls, tests, logging, and unresolved risks.

prompt_templates.title: Check One Endpoint
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this API endpoint: [details]. Identify authentication, authorization, validation, and error-handling gaps. Return prioritized recommendations and explain each risk.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner review of a single endpoint

prompt_templates.title: Design Secure Authentication
prompt_templates.prompt: Design authentication for [API type] serving [users]. Compare suitable methods, define token or session handling, and include revocation, rate limits, and failure responses.

prompt_templates.title: Assess an API Surface
prompt_templates.prompt: Assess these endpoints and data flows: [inventory]. Map risks to OWASP API categories. Identify missing object, property, and function authorization checks.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Security Test Plan
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a risk-based security test plan for [architecture]. Cover abuse cases, tenant isolation, token lifecycle, injection, resource consumption, logging, and release gates.

output_examples.input: Review a profile endpoint that accepts a user ID and returns account details.
output: High priority: enforce object-level authorization before loading the profile.
Validate the identifier format and return consistent not-found responses.
Select only approved response fields and exclude credentials or internal metadata.

output_examples.input: Recommend controls for a public login endpoint used by web and mobile clients.
output: Use uniform credential errors, secure password verification, and short-lived access tokens.
Apply account-aware and network-aware rate limits with monitored escalation.
Rotate refresh tokens, store token hashes, and revoke the token family after reuse.

output_examples.input: Prepare a release checklist for a new payments API.
output: Verify object and function authorization for every payment action.
Test schema validation, idempotency, replay protection, quotas, and safe errors.
Confirm audit logs exclude secrets while preserving actor, action, resource, and outcome.

best_practices: Provide the framework, endpoint inventory, identity model, trust boundaries, and sensitive data types.
Ask for findings prioritized by exploitability, impact, and implementation effort.
Validate generated recommendations with tests, current library documentation, and environment-specific threat models.
anti_patterns: Do not apply sample code unchanged without checking library versions and deployment assumptions.
Do not treat authentication as authorization or rely only on client-supplied identifiers.
Do not expose production secrets, tokens, personal data, or complete internal errors in prompts.

faq.question: Does this skill run a security scan?
faq.answer: No. It provides design, review, and testing guidance based on the context you supply.

faq.question: Which API styles does it cover?
faq.answer: It addresses REST, GraphQL, and WebSocket concerns, although most implementation examples use Node.js and Express.

faq.question: Can it design JWT authentication?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers signing, verification, expiry, refresh handling, protected routes, and related security checks.

faq.question: Does it cover authorization?
faq.answer: Yes. It explains role checks, ownership checks, protected routes, and OWASP object and function authorization risks.

faq.question: Can it prevent DDoS attacks?
faq.answer: It can recommend application rate limits and quotas, but complete DDoS protection also requires infrastructure and provider controls.

faq.question: Is its output sufficient for compliance?
faq.answer: No. Compliance requires scoped controls, evidence, testing, documentation, and qualified review for the applicable standard.
